rv.q: Seen on the deeper stage of the Helen Hayes, they look a little lonelier and more vulnerable than they did off Broadway, which helps to make “Next Fall” the funniest heartbreaker in town.
Don't let the lack of celebrity deter you.
Even if he does borrow poignant minor-key notes from Thornton Wilder (Luke played the Stage Manager in a memorable production of "Our Town"), Nauffts' play is genuinely affecting.
The playwright also shows a winning tenderness toward his characters, whether they’re being open-minded or unyielding, flip or earnest.

Last Updated: 5:04 AM, March 12, 2010. Posted: 3:38 AM, March 12, 2010 NEXT FALL Theatre, 240 W. 44th St.; 212-239-6200. Geoffrey Nauffts' play "Next Fall" cov ers at least two of this spring's theater trends: It centers on gay men, and it uses a jumbled timeline to tell the story.
I'm afraid I am not a believer - not in the love story or in the play.

No sooner does "The Temperamentals" become an episode of "Great Gays in History" than it grows painfully preachy, but until then it's a sharp-witted snapshot of a life that few who didn't live it can imagine.
Now this smart and enormously affecting gem has transferred to Broadway, and it’s made a believer of me all over again.

Sheryl Kaller’s direction is savvy enough, as are Jess Goldstein’s costumes. Wilson Chin’s set design contends valiantly with the frequent changes of locale, and the acting is mostly good. Only Adam’s intended charm seems to me undercut by Patrick Breen’s machine-gun delivery and cadaverous looks.
Parks throws a variety of theatrical surprises into this situation, but they tend, rather more surprisingly, not to alter it.
Unfortunately, those touches never blossom into meaningful or convincing explorations.

By treating Luke and his family's views with so little respect and sensitivity, and never providing a hint of a considered defense of what they believe and why, the entire endeavor becomes meaningless.

Lacking big-name stars, Geoffrey Nauffts' play is going to be a tough sell. But anyone interested in quality theater would do well to check out this deeply moving and surprisingly funny work at the Theater.
Sheryl Kaller's production showcases sensitive performances that capture the heart and sadness inherent in the play.
It is appalling that in this day and age, there is no way of communicating to the actors 'It's not you, it's the play,' as one storms out of the theatre.
Frankly I could scarcely wait to move myself out of the theater and into a martini.

cn.t: Critics are divided on this gay relationship drama about faith and love. Some praise its smart, moving exploration of complex characters, while others dismiss it as derivative, mawkish tearjerker material that lost intimacy in its Broadway transfer.

sg.ra: Multiple guides converge on Rows B to H center as the best views in Broadway's smallest house (597 seats), where the intimate scale means these seats feel closer to the stage than premium orchestra in any other Broadway theater. The Hayes-specific tradeoff: patrons repeatedly flag that the stage sits unusually high for such an intimate room, so Row A and the very front can force neck-craning — one AVFMS viewer described the Hayes stage as 'particularly high for the first couple of rows, so you'll be using your neck to look up,' and a JOB patron noted 'The stage is high so you don't see actors' feet.' Rows B-H sit far enough back to clear that stage-height issue while still letting you read facial expressions in a house this small.

sg.vl: Value sweet spot where the rake kicks in
sg.ra: Rows F-M center are consistently flagged as the value band at Hayes — priced below premium but still close in a 597-seat room. The Hayes-specific reason to favor the back half of that band (J-M) over F-I: an AVFMS reviewer explicitly observed that 'Row J in the orchestra level is where the rake of the floor starts to increase so even a short guy like me can see over someone tall.' That makes J-M the first rows where a tall head in front stops being a problem, which matters more at Hayes than at larger houses because the orchestra is 'more long than it is wide' (NYTix) and the stage height is tall, so front-orchestra sightlines are flatter than usual.

The very back row of the Hayes mezzanine sits directly against the theater's staff/operations area — a quirk specific to this post-2018-renovation layout. Multiple AVFMS reviewers independently complain the ushers or crew are audible throughout the show from Mezz Row J: one wrote 'this row butts up against the row where the theater staff sits and they chatted, loudly, throughout the show'; another said 'the ushers downstairs were loud and I could sometimes hear their murmurings'; an accessible-seat user at Mezz J-101 reported 'there's some sort of operation booth to the right of this seat and it's very loud and distracting. I could hear talking and typing throughout the entire show.' Because Hayes is the smallest house on Broadway, there's no orchestra noise to mask ambient staff chatter the way a 1,500-seat venue would — in this intimate room, the booth chatter carries.
